paragraphs.text: Glycogenosis type II (Pompe disease) is a progressive, debilitating and often fatal neuromuscular disorder. Its clinical phenotypes form a continuum that varies in which organs are involved, age at onset and severity (Bembi et al., 2008). The late-onset form, which includes juvenile- and adult-onset cases, is marked by slowly progressive proximal muscle weakness that mainly affects the pelvic girdle, together with respiratory insufficiency due to diaphragmatic weakness (Trend et al., 1985; Laforêt et al., 2000). Residual acid maltase activity is found in muscle from patients with the late-onset form (Mehler and DiMauro, 1977).

paragraphs.text: Forsha et al. (2011) evaluated baseline ECGs and echocardiograms in 87 adults with late-onset Pompe disease enrolled in a randomized trial of enzyme replacement therapy. There were 44 males and 43 females with a median age of 44 years, and 82 were Caucasian. Forty-six percent had 1 or more abnormalities. The most frequent were left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) by ECG (12%), a short PR interval (10%) and decreased ejection fraction (7%). Six patients had a left ventricular ejection fraction of less than 55% (range, 41 to 54%). Only 4 patients (5%) had an elevated left ventricular mass index on echocardiogram, all in the mild range. The severe ventricular hypertrophy typical of infantile Pompe disease was not seen. Other findings included sinus tachycardia, prolonged QTc interval, bundle branch block, atrial enlargement, and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome in 2 patients. No patient had atrioventricular block, right ventricular hypertrophy or ventricular tachycardia. The authors noted that the abnormalities might be due to Pompe disease or to comorbid conditions.

paragraphs.text: Herbert et al. (2019) found that 4 of 84 patients (4.8%) followed at their center for late-onset Pompe disease with the c.-32-13T-G GAA variant had been clinically diagnosed with symptoms beginning in the first 2 years of life (10 days to 20 months). Initial symptoms included delayed gross motor milestones, proximal weakness, swallowing and feeding difficulties, and sleep apnea. All 4 patients were Caucasian. Patient 1, a boy, presented at 5 months with delayed motor development and feeding difficulties, and had elevated CK, ALT and AST. He had generalized hypotonia, head lag when pulled to sit, myopathic facies and hypertrophied calf muscles. He later had swallowing difficulty with aspiration, obstructive and central apneas, motor regression, myotonic discharges on EMG, progressive scoliosis requiring surgery, and mild ptosis of the left eye. Patient 2, a girl and one of fraternal twins, was born at term and presented on day 10 of life with poor feeding, lethargy and vomiting. She later had difficulty swallowing saliva, persistent gastroesophageal reflux requiring a gastrostomy tube, urinary retention, chronic constipation, a hypernasal voice, aspiration pneumonia and apneic episodes during sleep. Patient 3, a boy, had difficulty sitting unsupported and holding his head upright at 6 months, and at 12 months had an unsteady wide-based gait and frequent falls. He later had a Gowers sign, scapular winging, scoliosis with a Cobb angle of 40 degrees, hypernasality, lingual weakness, hyporeflexia and mild ptosis. Patient 4, a girl born preterm at 36 weeks, needed brief CPAP in the newborn period for apnea and bradycardia. She had delayed motor milestones, leg pain, a Gowers sign, a waddling gait, lumbar lordosis, bilateral winged scapulae, and snoring with apneic pauses. Cardiac evaluations, including ECG and echocardiography, were normal in all 4 patients. Despite enzyme replacement therapy, all had residual muscle weakness.

paragraphs.text: Raben et al. (1998) generated mice homozygous for a targeted disruption of the Gaa gene (6neo/6neo). The mice lacked enzyme activity and accumulated glycogen in cardiac and skeletal muscle lysosomes by 3 weeks of age, and their mobility and strength were markedly reduced by 3.5 weeks. They grew normally, reached adulthood and remained fertile. As in the human adult disease, older mice accumulated glycogen in the diaphragm, and by 8 to 9 months they had obvious muscle wasting and a weak, waddling gait. A second model, mice with deletion of exon 6 (Delta6/Delta6), had unimpaired strength and mobility up to 6.5 months of age, although their biochemical and pathologic changes were indistinguishable from those of the 6neo/6neo mice. The authors suggested that the genetic background of the mouse strains contributed to the differences between the models.
